passage:
I'm Eshaan. Last year I got an offer for a design course in Pune. Papa had other plans: engineering, like him, like his father. He'd taken a loan for my coaching. When I told him about the design course, he didn't shout. He just said, "So all that was for nothing." Mummy said, "He means we gave up so much for our son, beta." My brother Mridul told me later that Papa sat on the terrace till midnight.
I understood it then. To them, my choice wasn't about a course. It felt like I was saying no to everything they had done for me, and to the family way. I wasn't. I just wanted to draw. But it took us months to hear each other.

qa.q: What course did Eshaan get an offer for?
qa.a: He got an offer for a design course in Pune.

qa.q: What was Papa feeling when he said, "So all that was for nothing"?
qa.a: He seemed hurt and let down, feeling that Eshaan's choice rejected the loan, the coaching and the family tradition.

qa.q: What could Eshaan have said to ease the clash?
qa.a: He could have told his parents clearly that he valued their sacrifice and wasn't rejecting them, and explained why design mattered to him.

qa.q: How did Mridul experience the conflict?
qa.a: He was a worried witness in between, noticing their father sitting on the terrace till midnight and later telling Eshaan.

grounding: It shows a young man's choice of course clashing with his father's plan, which carries sacrifice and expectation, so the choice feels like rejecting the family.

passage:
Supervisor's note, summer internship programme.
Aditi, one of our best interns, received a full-time offer from our Bengaluru office today. At lunch I saw her on the phone in the corridor. I could hear her mother's voice rising. Aditi kept saying, "Ma, it's just a job, it's not about leaving you." Her mother said something about the shop, and her father's health, and how they had planned for Aditi to join the family business in Nashik. Aditi came back with red eyes. She told me, "They think I'm choosing strangers over them."
I told her she didn't have to decide today. I gave her the HR contact to ask for more time, and suggested she talk with her parents face to face.
— Ishita, programme lead

qa.q: Which office did Aditi get an offer from?
qa.a: She got a full-time offer from the Bengaluru office.

qa.q: What does Aditi's line "They think I'm choosing strangers over them" show about her feelings?
qa.a: It shows she feels misunderstood and sad, since her parents take her job choice as rejecting the family and its plans.

qa.q: What support did Ishita offer at this stage?
qa.a: Ishita told Aditi there was no need to decide today, helped Aditi ask for more time and suggested a face-to-face talk, giving room for a calmer conversation.

qa.q: How might Aditi's mother see the Bengaluru offer?
qa.a: She may see it as a loss of the future they planned together, and worry about the shop and her husband's health without Aditi.

grounding: It illustrates a clash over a job in another city, where the family's plan and sacrifice make the young woman's choice feel like a rejection.

passage:
I told my parents about Zubin on a Sunday, after lunch, because I thought full stomachs might help. They didn't.

Mummy put her cup down. Papa looked at the wall. Then Mummy said, very quietly, "We sent you to that college. We took a loan. We turned down your chacha's help so no one could say anything. And now you want to marry a boy we've never met, from another community?"

I tried to explain: he's kind, he's studying law, his family is lovely. But I could see that every word sounded to them like I was rejecting everything they'd done for me.

Papa finally said, "We had a plan for you." That was the worst part. Not the anger. The plan. As if I were a project that had gone off course.

I wasn't rejecting them. I was choosing someone. I didn't know how to make them see the difference.

— Sarika

qa.q: What is Zubin studying?
qa.a: Law.

qa.q: How did Sarika feel when Papa said they had a plan?
qa.a: Sarika felt hurt most by Papa's words "We had a plan for you", feeling treated like a project that had gone off course.

qa.q: What could Sarika try next?
qa.a: Separate the two things for Sarika's parents: say their sacrifices are valued and this isn't a rejection, and suggest they meet Zubin before deciding.

qa.q: How do Sarika's parents seem to see her choice?
qa.a: They seem to feel hurt and rejected, since their sacrifices and plans made Sarika's choice feel like a rejection of the family.

grounding: Sarika tells her parents about a partner from another community, and because their plan carries sacrifice and expectation, her choice feels to them like rejection.

passage:
Student counsellor's note, Friday

Pankaj, first-year engineering, came to see me today. He wants to switch to a design course next year. His father has said no.

Pankaj described the argument: his father reminded him that the family sold land to pay his coaching fees for two years, and that his grandfather had always wanted an engineer in the family. "If you leave engineering, you're telling us everything we did was for nothing."

Pankaj said he feels torn: grateful and guilty, but also sure he is unhappy. He cried when he said, "I'm not rejecting them. I just want to choose my own work."

We discussed how his father may be hearing the choice as a rejection of the family's sacrifice. I suggested Pankaj begin by thanking his father for what he gave up, before explaining his reasons. We will meet again next week.

— Saurabh Mehta, counsellor

qa.q: What did the family sell to pay for Pankaj's coaching?
qa.a: Land.

qa.q: How does Pankaj feel about switching courses?
qa.a: He feels torn: grateful and guilty for the family's sacrifice, but sure he is unhappy in engineering.

qa.q: Why might starting with thanks help Pankaj's next conversation?
qa.a: His father hears the switch as a rejection of the sacrifice; acknowledging it first may help his father listen to Pankaj's reasons.

qa.q: How does Pankaj's father see the choice?
qa.a: He sees it as saying the family's sacrifice was for nothing, so it feels like a rejection of the family.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows Pankaj clashing with his father over a course, where the family's sacrifice and expectations make his choice feel like rejection.

passage:
Wednesday night

I got the job in Bengaluru. The one I've wanted since second year. I told Ammi and Abbu at dinner, and I was so happy I didn't see it coming.

Ammi put her spoon down. "Bengaluru? Alone? We thought you'd work here, near us. Near Sabina."

Sabina is my little sister. She's only twelve. Ammi's been saying for years that I'd help raise her.

Abbu said, "We didn't send you to college so you could leave." He didn't shout. He just looked tired.

And suddenly I felt like I'd done something terrible. Like choosing a job was the same as choosing to abandon them.

I'm not abandoning anyone. I'd come home every holiday. I'd call every day. But to them, Bengaluru sounds like goodbye.

I haven't accepted the offer yet. I have until Friday.

— Ayesha

qa.q: How old is Sabina?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel after Abbu's words at dinner?
qa.a: Ayesha felt suddenly guilty, as if choosing the job was the same as abandoning the family, after being so happy.

qa.q: What could Ayesha try before Friday?
qa.a: Talk calmly with Ammi and Abbu about their fears and how Ayesha would stay close, with calls and visits, before deciding.

qa.q: How do Ammi and Abbu seem to see the job in Bengaluru?
qa.a: They see it as goodbye, a rejection of their plan that Ayesha would stay near and help raise Sabina.

grounding: Ayesha's job offer in another city clashes with her parents' plan, and because it carries family expectations, her choice feels to them like a rejection.

Baba: Saw your mail. Bengaluru?? You didn't even discuss.
Arnab: I'm discussing now. It's a good offer, Baba. Product design, what I studied for.
Baba: We sent you to engineering so you could join Mitra Uncle's firm here. He has kept the seat for you.
Arnab: I never said I wanted that seat.
Baba: Your Ma sold her gold bangles for your first-year fees. Did you forget?
Arnab: I haven't forgotten anything. That's not fair.
Baba: Fair? We built everything around you. Now you want to go two thousand kilometres away.
Arnab: I'm not rejecting you. I'm choosing a job.
Baba: From here it feels the same.
Arnab to Jomon, a minute later: he thinks I'm leaving the family, not Kolkata 😔
Jomon: give him a day. then call, don't type 🙏

qa.q: Where is the job offer Arnab mentions?
qa.a: In Bengaluru, in product design.

qa.q: What is Arnab feeling when Baba mentions the gold bangles?
qa.a: Arnab feels guilty and hurt, and calls it unfair, because the family's sacrifice is being used to make the job feel like a betrayal.

qa.q: What would help at this stage of the clash?
qa.a: Following Jomon's advice, waiting a day and then calling instead of typing, so Arnab can honour the family's sacrifice while explaining the choice.

qa.q: How does Baba see Arnab's decision?
qa.a: To Baba it feels like a rejection of the family and everything they built around Arnab, not just a move to another city.

grounding: Shows a clash over a job in another city, where the parent's plan carries family sacrifice so the young adult's choice feels like rejection.
